name: Eyelid revision surgery

card.summary: A corrective operation performed after an earlier eyelid surgery to fix a fold that is too high, scarred, asymmetric or otherwise unsatisfactory, restoring a more natural eye appearance.
card.note: Revision is generally more technically demanding than primary surgery; outcomes are reported mostly in retrospective surgeon series.

quick.overview:
Eyelid revision surgery is a second (or later) operation on eyelids that were previously operated on, done to correct problems such as a double-eyelid fold set too high, depressed scars, extra folds, asymmetry, drooping or fullness. The payoff is a more natural, balanced eye area, which many people see as central to how open and symmetrical the face looks.

Surgeons describe it as one of the harder procedures in oculoplastic practice, because scar tissue and altered anatomy have to be worked through. Published results are mostly retrospective case series from surgeons in Asia and elsewhere, reporting that most patients see the problem reduced.
quick.how: A consultation reviews the original surgery, photographs from several positions, and what the person wants changed. Surgeons then choose a technique matched to the problem, such as lowering a high fold with tissue flaps or repositioning orbital fat, or releasing and refilling depressed scars. Recovery involves swelling and bruising for several weeks, and final shape is judged after healing.
quick.risks: Reported risks include persistent asymmetry, scarring, eyelid malposition or ptosis, dry-eye symptoms and the possibility of further revision. A case report in the literature describes a patient with borderline personality disorder who harmed her own eyelids after a surgeon declined further revision, and surgeons describe screening for body-image distress as part of care.

lead: Eyelid revision surgery, or revision (secondary) blepharoplasty, is surgery to correct unsatisfactory results of an earlier eyelid operation. Reasons surgeons list for dissatisfaction include scars, a fold that is too low or too high, a fold that is too shallow or too deep, triple folds, pretarsal fullness, ptosis and asymmetry.[1][2]

People pursue revision to get a more natural, symmetric eye area, since the eyes are a focal point of the face. The most common request described in Asian blepharoplasty literature is a fold that sits too high after double-eyelid surgery, which is described as difficult to correct.[3][4]

Evidence consists mainly of retrospective surgical series. One series of 213 secondary operations for high folds reported that nearly all cases (98.59%) achieved a smaller fold.[3] Other series report on depressed scars and on flap and fat-repositioning techniques.[4][5][6]

chain: Identify the problem from the prior surgery
Surgeon corrects fold height, scar or asymmetry
angle.text: Revision surgery works directly on the eyelid tissue to lower or raise a fold, release scars and even out asymmetry. People who are unhappy with a prior blepharoplasty use it to get the eye shape they originally wanted.

Swelling and bruising over several weeks

paras: Blepharoplasty reshapes the eyelids by removing or repositioning skin, muscle and fat, and the upper-eyelid incision is designed to heal within the natural fold.[7] Revision procedures reoperate on a prior result, and a 2013 review in Clinics in Plastic Surgery covers the complications that lead to them and the surgical and nonsurgical options for correcting them.[1]

A 2015 review of revision double-eyelid surgery lists scars, low or high folds, shallow or deep folds, triple folds, pretarsal fullness, ptosis and asymmetry, and notes that the ideal fold height varies by patient and culture.[2]

Depressed scarring after incisional upper blepharoplasty is described as a frequent contributor to dissatisfaction and a challenge for oculoplastic surgeons.[6] Lower-eyelid revisions and tear-trough corrections have also been reported using direct infraorbital incisions.[8]

For a high fold, surgeons have described using a pretarsal orbicularis oculi flap, tarsus-orbicularis fixation combined with orbital fat repositioning, and other approaches to lower the fold.[3][4][5] For depressed scars, a 2024 study described a turnover orbicularis-septum composite flap after releasing scar adhesions.[6]

Planning relies on standardised photography from several positions to document the eyelids at rest and in motion.[9] Regional nerve block anaesthesia has been proposed in place of local infiltration to reduce swelling and distortion that can complicate intraoperative assessment.[10]

Recovery includes swelling and bruising that generally resolve over several weeks.[7] Revisions are described as more demanding than primary surgery, with outcomes that vary with anatomy and technique.[1][5]

Psychological factors appear in the literature: a case report describes a patient with borderline personality disorder who removed her own upper eyelids after a surgeon declined further revision, and the authors contrast preoccupation in that condition with body dysmorphic disorder.[11]

Studies are mostly retrospective surgeon series. In a 4-year series of 213 secondary blepharoplasties for high folds, almost all cases achieved fold reduction (98.59%).[3] A retrospective study of 31 Chinese patients treated with a pretarsal orbicularis oculi flap evaluated aesthetic outcomes.[4] A study of 86 patients (154 eyelids) used tarsus-orbicularis fixation with fat repositioning for high folds,[5] and a retrospective study of 118 patients examined a flap technique for depressed scars.[6]
